title: Elementary Statistics for Social Sciences II
text:
Preface
This book covers the first half of 208272 Elementary Statistics for Social Sciences II: the principles of statistical inference, inference about means, proportions and variances, and analysis of variance. All examples use economic contexts. Unless a source is given, the numbers in the examples are hypothetical and are used for illustration only.

title: Elementary Statistics for Social Sciences II
section: The five steps of a hypothesis test
text:
The five steps of a hypothesis test

Hypotheses: state \(H_0\) and \(H_1\).
Level of significance: state \(\alpha\).
Test statistic: write the formula, substitute the values, and give the result.
Critical value and critical region.
Decision and interpretation.

title: Elementary Statistics for Social Sciences II
text:
Writing the conclusion
Decision using the critical region (Chapters 1–2 and Section 3.1)

\(t_{\text{cal}}\) = … [falls / does not fall] in the critical region (\(t_{\text{cal}}\) [<, >] …), so we [reject / accept] \(H_0\).

Decision using the p-value (from Section 3.2 onward)

p-value = … [<, \(\ge\)] \(\alpha\) = 0.05, so we [reject / accept] \(H_0\).

Interpretation

That is, … at the 0.05 level of significance.


If we reject \(H_0\), write \(H_1\) as a sentence.
If we accept \(H_0\), write \(H_0\) as a sentence.
For a two-sided test that rejects \(H_0\), also state the direction, using the sample statistic.

Confidence interval

We are 95% confident that … is between … and ….

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
text:
Learning Objectives
After this chapter you should be able to:
crumbs: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
text:
Distinguish a parameter from a statistic.
Describe the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) and of \(\hat{p}\): its mean, its standard error and its shape.
Use the Central Limit Theorem to find probabilities about \(\bar{x}\) and \(\hat{p}\).
Explain what a 95% confidence interval means.
Write the null and alternative hypotheses for a research question, and tell a one-sided test from a two-sided test.
Find critical values and the critical region from the \(z\) table (Table 4).
Explain Type I and Type II errors in an economic setting.







NoteWhy Does This Matter?



Economists rarely see a whole population. The Ministry of Labour cannot ask every worker in Chiang Mai about their wage, and the Bank of Thailand cannot survey every household about its debt. Instead we take a sample and use it to say something about the population.
Two samples from the same population give different answers. Statistical inference tells us how much a sample result can vary, and so how far we can trust it. This chapter builds the ideas used in every later chapter.
crumbs: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
text:
1.1 Parameters, Statistics and Sampling Distributions
A parameter describes a population. It is a fixed number, but usually unknown. A statistic describes a sample. We can calculate it, but it changes from sample to sample.




Population (parameter)
Sample (statistic)




Mean
\(\mu\)
\(\bar{x}\)


Standard deviation
\(\sigma\)
\(s\)


Variance
\(\sigma^2\)
\(s^2\)


Proportion
\(p\)
\(\hat{p}\)


Size
\(N\)
\(n\)



The sampling distribution of a statistic is the distribution of its values over all possible samples of the same size \(n\).


Show R code
set.seed(272)
income_pop <- rlnorm(100000, meanlog = log(22000), sdlog = 0.65)
mu_inc <- mean(income_pop)
sd_inc <- sd(income_pop)

sim_means <- function(n, reps = 5000) {
  replicate(reps, mean(sample(income_pop, n)))
}
samp <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = "Population", value = income_pop),
  data.frame(panel = "Means, n = 5", value = sim_means(5)),
  data.frame(panel = "Means, n = 30", value = sim_means(30)),
  data.frame(panel = "Means, n = 100", value = sim_means(100))
)
samp$panel <- factor(samp$panel, levels = c("Population", "Means, n = 5",
                                            "Means, n = 30", "Means, n = 100"))


Example. Figure 1.1 uses a hypothetical population of 100,000 households. Monthly household income is skewed to the right: most households earn a moderate amount and a few earn a great deal. The population mean is \(\mu\) = 27,054 baht and the standard deviation is \(\sigma\) = 19,543 baht. The other panels show the means of 5,000 random samples of size 5, 30 and 100.


Show R code
ggplot(samp, aes(value / 1000)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_inc / 1000, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Monthly income (thousand baht)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())








Figure 1.1: Household income in a hypothetical population (top left) and the sampling distribution of the sample mean for n = 5, 30 and 100





Three things happen as \(n\) grows:

The sample means are centred on the population mean \(\mu\) (dashed line).
The spread of the sample means gets smaller.
The shape gets closer to a normal curve, even though the population is skewed.

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
section: 1.2 Standard Error and the Central Limit Theorem
text:
1.2 Standard Error and the Central Limit Theorem
The standard deviation of a sampling distribution is called the standard error (SE). It measures how much a statistic varies from sample to sample.

Sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\)

Mean: \(\mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu\)
Standard error: \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
Shape:

if the population is normal, \(\bar{x}\) is normal for any \(n\);
if not, \(\bar{x}\) is approximately normal when \(n\) is large (\(n \ge 30\)). This is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).


So we can standardize \(\bar{x}\) and use the \(z\) table: \[
z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}
\]


Sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\)
The sample proportion \(\hat{p} = x/n\), where \(x\) is the number of “successes”.

Mean: \(\mu_{\hat{p}} = p\)
Standard error: \(\displaystyle \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\)
Shape: approximately normal when \(np \ge 5\) and \(n(1-p) \ge 5\).

\[
z = \frac{\hat{p} - p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}
\]






TipLarger samples, smaller error



Because \(\sqrt{n}\) is in the denominator, a sample four times as large halves the standard error.




Show R code
w_mu <- 380; w_sigma <- 60; w_n <- 36
w_se <- w_sigma / sqrt(w_n)
w_z  <- (400 - w_mu) / w_se
w_F  <- round(pnorm(w_z), 4)

d_p <- 0.65; d_n <- 400
d_se <- round(sqrt(d_p * (1 - d_p) / d_n), 4)
d_z  <- round((0.60 - d_p) / d_se, 2)
d_F  <- round(pnorm(abs(d_z)), 4)




Worked Example 1.1: daily wage
Suppose the daily wage of construction workers in Chiang Mai has mean \(\mu\) = 380 baht and standard deviation \(\sigma\) = 60 baht (hypothetical figures). A random sample of \(n\) = 36 workers is taken.

Describe the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\).
Find the probability that the sample mean wage is more than 400 baht.







TipSolution






Since \(n\) = 36 \(\ge 30\), by the CLT \(\bar{x}\) is approximately normal with \[
\mu_{\bar{x}} = 380, \qquad
\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{60}{\sqrt{36}} = 10 \text{ baht.}
\]
\[
z = \frac{400 - 380}{10} = 2.00
\] From Table 4, \(P(Z \le 2.00) = 0.9772\), so \[
P(\bar{x} > 400) = P(Z > 2.00) = 1 - 0.9772 = 0.0228.
\]

About 2.3% of samples of 36 workers would have a mean wage above 400 baht.





Worked Example 1.2: household debt
Suppose 65% of households in a region have outstanding debt (hypothetical figure). A survey samples \(n\) = 400 households. Find the probability that less than 60% of the sampled households have debt.






TipSolution





Check the conditions: \(np = 260 \ge 5\) and \(n(1-p) = 140 \ge 5\), so \(\hat{p}\) is approximately normal. \[
\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.65(1-0.65)}{400}} = 0.0238
\] \[
z = \frac{0.60 - 0.65}{0.0238} = -2.10
\] Table 4 gives only positive \(z\). By symmetry, \[
P(\hat{p} < 0.60) = P(Z < -2.10) = P(Z > 2.10)
= 1 - 0.9821 = 0.0179.
\]





Show R code
y_mu <- 4500; y_sigma <- 900; y_n <- 81
y_se <- y_sigma / sqrt(y_n)
y_z  <- (4320 - y_mu) / y_se
y_F  <- round(pnorm(abs(y_z)), 4)

v_p <- 0.40; v_n <- 600
v_se <- round(sqrt(v_p * (1 - v_p) / v_n), 4)
v_z  <- round((0.45 - v_p) / v_se, 2)
v_F  <- round(pnorm(v_z), 4)




Your Turn






NoteYour Turn 1.1



The monthly rent of rooms near a university has mean 4,500 baht and standard deviation 900 baht (hypothetical figures). A random sample of 81 rooms is taken. Find

the standard error of \(\bar{x}\), and
the probability that the sample mean rent is less than 4,320 baht.









TipSolution: Your Turn 1.1






\(\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 900 / \sqrt{81} = 100\) baht.
\(z = (4320 - 4500) / 100 = -1.80\), so \(P(\bar{x} < 4320) = P(Z > 1.80) = 1 - 0.9641 = 0.0359\).










NoteYour Turn 1.2



In a province, 40% of workers are in the informal sector (hypothetical figure). A labour force survey samples 600 workers. Find the probability that more than 45% of the sample work in the informal sector.








TipSolution: Your Turn 1.2





\(np = 240\) and \(n(1-p) = 360\) are both at least 5. \(\sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{0.4(0.6)/600} = 0.0200\), \(z = (0.45 - 0.4)/0.0200 = 2.50\), so \(P(\hat{p} > 0.45) = 1 - 0.9938 = 0.0062\).

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
section: 1.3 The Idea of a Confidence Interval
text:
1.3 The Idea of a Confidence Interval
A single number such as \(\bar{x}\) is a point estimate. It is almost never exactly equal to \(\mu\). A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of plausible values instead: \[
\text{point estimate} \;\pm\; (\text{critical value}) \times \text{SE}
\]
The confidence level (for example 95%) describes the method, not one interval: if we took many samples and built a 95% CI from each, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true parameter.


Show R code
set.seed(2721)
z975 <- crit_z(0.975)
cis <- data.frame(sample = 1:40,
                  xbar = replicate(40, mean(rnorm(w_n, w_mu, w_sigma))))
cis$lower <- cis$xbar - z975 * w_se
cis$upper <- cis$xbar + z975 * w_se
cis$covers <- cis$lower <= w_mu & cis$upper >= w_mu
n_miss <- sum(!cis$covers)
ggplot(cis, aes(y = sample, xmin = lower, xmax = upper, colour = covers)) +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xbar), size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = w_mu, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey30", `FALSE` = "firebrick"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Daily wage (baht)", y = "Sample")








Figure 1.2: Forty 95% confidence intervals for the mean daily wage, each from a different sample of 36 workers (hypothetical population with mean 380 baht). Red intervals miss the true mean.





In Figure 1.2, 37 of the 40 intervals contain \(\mu\) = 380 and 3 do not. For a single interval we write:

We are 95% confident that the mean daily wage is between … and … baht.







WarningA common mistake



Do not say “there is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) is in this interval”. Once the interval is calculated, \(\mu\) is either in it or not. The 95% refers to how often the method works.


Chapters 2 and 3 give the formula of the CI for each parameter.

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
text:
1.4 The Logic of Hypothesis Testing
A hypothesis test uses sample data to decide between two statements about a population parameter.

The null hypothesis \(H_0\) is the statement of “no change” or “no difference”. It always contains the equals sign.
The alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) is what the researcher wants to show. It contains \(\ne\), \(<\) or \(>\).

We assume \(H_0\) is true and ask whether the sample result is unusual under that assumption. If it is, we reject \(H_0\).
Example. The Ministry of Labour reports that the mean daily wage of construction workers is 380 baht. A labour union believes the mean is lower. \[
H_0: \mu = 380 \qquad H_1: \mu < 380
\]
The direction in \(H_1\) comes from the research question, never from the data.









Research question
\(H_1\)
Test
Critical region




Is it different from \(\mu_0\)?
\(\mu \ne \mu_0\)
two-sided
both tails, area \(\alpha/2\) each


Is it less than \(\mu_0\)?
\(\mu < \mu_0\)
one-sided (left)
left tail, area \(\alpha\)


Is it greater than \(\mu_0\)?
\(\mu > \mu_0\)
one-sided (right)
right tail, area \(\alpha\)




Test statistic, critical value and critical region

The test statistic measures how far the sample result is from \(H_0\), in standard errors. For example \(z_{\text{cal}} = (\bar{x} - \mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})\).
The level of significance \(\alpha\) is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true. We usually use \(\alpha\) = 0.05.
The critical value separates the values of the test statistic that lead to rejecting \(H_0\) from those that do not.
The critical region is the set of values that lead to rejecting \(H_0\).


Show R code
crit_plot("z", "two")
crit_plot("z", "left")
crit_plot("z", "right")












(a) Two-sided











(b) Left-sided











(c) Right-sided







Figure 1.3: Critical regions for a z test at alpha = 0.05



Decision rule. If \(z_{\text{cal}}\) falls in the critical region, we reject \(H_0\). Otherwise we accept \(H_0\).


Writing the hypotheses
Worked Example 1.3. Write \(H_0\) and \(H_1\).

A price-monitoring agency checks whether the mean price of a 5-kg bag of rice has changed from 210 baht.
An economist claims that more than 30% of households in Chiang Mai have used a government stimulus measure.
A bank claims that the mean monthly loan payment of its customers is less than 8,000 baht.







TipSolution






\(H_0: \mu = 210 \quad H_1: \mu \ne 210\) (two-sided: “changed” has no direction)
\(H_0: p = 0.30 \quad H_1: p > 0.30\) (right-sided)
\(H_0: \mu = 8000 \quad H_1: \mu < 8000\) (left-sided)










NoteYour Turn 1.3



Write \(H_0\) and \(H_1\), and say whether each test is two-sided, left-sided or right-sided.

A researcher tests whether the mean household debt in a district is higher than 200,000 baht.
An analyst tests whether the proportion of firms that raised prices last quarter is different from 0.50.
A manager tests whether a new pricing strategy has reduced the mean number of days a product stays in stock below 14 days.









TipSolution: Your Turn 1.3






\(H_0: \mu = 200000 \quad H_1: \mu > 200000\) (right-sided)
\(H_0: p = 0.50 \quad H_1: p \ne 0.50\) (two-sided)
\(H_0: \mu = 14 \quad H_1: \mu < 14\) (left-sided)

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
section: 1.5 Type I and Type II Errors
text:
1.5 Type I and Type II Errors
The decision is based on a sample, so it can be wrong.









\(H_0\) is true
\(H_0\) is false




Reject \(H_0\)
Type I error (probability \(\alpha\))
Correct decision


Accept \(H_0\)
Correct decision
Type II error (probability \(\beta\))



Example. The government tests whether a stimulus measure increased mean household spending. \(H_0\): the measure had no effect; \(H_1\): the measure increased spending.

Type I error: concluding that the measure worked when it did not. The government may continue an expensive policy that has no effect.
Type II error: concluding that the measure did not work when it did. The government may stop a useful policy.







TipChoosing \(\alpha\)



A smaller \(\alpha\) makes a Type I error less likely but a Type II error more likely, for the same sample size. A larger sample reduces both.
crumbs: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
text:
1.6 Reading Statistical Tables
All the tables used in this course (Tables 4–7) give the area to the left of a value. The subscript in our notation is that area: \(z_{0.975}\) is the value with area 0.975 to its left.






ImportantTwo steps for every critical value




Draw the curve and shade the area to the left of the value you need.
Read the table at that left-tail area.



The \(z\) table (Table 4) gives \(P(Z \le z)\) for \(z\) from 0.00 to 3.49. The bottom row also lists the most common values:


Show R code

title: 1  Basic Principles of Statistical Inference
text:
Exercises
1.1 The price of a kilogram of pork at fresh markets has mean 45 baht and standard deviation 4 baht (hypothetical figures). A random sample of 64 markets is taken.

Find the standard error of \(\bar{x}\).
Find \(P(\bar{x} < 44.2)\).
Find \(P(44.2 < \bar{x} < 46)\).







TipSolution: Exercise 1.1






\(\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 4/\sqrt{64} = 0.5\) baht.
\(z = (44.2 - 45)/0.5 = -1.60\); \(P(\bar{x} < 44.2) = 1 - 0.9452 = 0.0548\).
\(z = (46 - 45)/0.5 = 2.00\); \(P(44.2 < \bar{x} < 46) = 0.9772 - 0.0548 = 0.9224\).




1.2 Write \(H_0\) and \(H_1\).

The Bank of Thailand tests whether mean headline inflation over the past year was above its 3% upper target.
A researcher tests whether the proportion of graduates who find a job within six months differs from 0.70.
A firm tests whether a discount campaign reduced the mean time to sell a product below 20 days.







TipSolution: Exercise 1.2






\(H_0: \mu = 3 \quad H_1: \mu > 3\)
\(H_0: p = 0.70 \quad H_1: p \ne 0.70\)
\(H_0: \mu = 20 \quad H_1: \mu < 20\)




1.3 Find the critical value(s) and the critical region of a \(z\) test.

\(H_1: \mu \ne \mu_0\), \(\alpha\) = 0.10
\(H_1: \mu < \mu_0\), \(\alpha\) = 0.01
\(H_1: p > p_0\), \(\alpha\) = 0.05







TipSolution: Exercise 1.3






\(z_{0.95} = 1.645\): reject \(H_0\) if \(z_{\text{cal}} < -1.645\) or \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.645\).
\(z_{0.01} = -z_{0.99} = -2.326\): reject \(H_0\) if \(z_{\text{cal}} < -2.326\).
\(z_{0.95} = 1.645\): reject \(H_0\) if \(z_{\text{cal}} > 1.645\).




1.4 A provincial office tests whether a job-training programme raised the mean monthly income of participants. \(H_0\): the programme has no effect on mean income; \(H_1\): the programme raises mean income. Describe a Type I error and a Type II error in this context, and give one consequence of each.






TipSolution: Exercise 1.4





Type I error: concluding that the programme raises income when it does not. Budget may continue to be spent on a programme that does not work. Type II error: concluding that the programme has no effect when it does raise income. A useful programme may be cut.



1.5 The unemployment rate in a province is 5% (hypothetical figure). Can the normal approximation be used for \(\hat{p}\) when (a) \(n\) = 80, (b) \(n\) = 200? Explain.






TipSolution: Exercise 1.5






\(np = 80(0.05) = 4 < 5\), so the normal approximation should not be used.
\(np = 200(0.05) = 10\) and \(n(1-p) = 190\) are both at least 5, so it can be used.




1.6 A 95% CI for the mean monthly electricity bill of households in a city is 1,120 to 1,280 baht. Which statements are correct?

We are 95% confident that the mean monthly electricity bill of all households in the city is between 1,120 and 1,280 baht.
95% of households in the city pay between 1,120 and 1,280 baht per month.
If we took many samples and built a 95% CI from each, about 95% of the intervals would contain the population mean.







TipSolution: Exercise 1.6






and (c) are correct. (b) is wrong: the interval is about the population mean, not about individual households.
